title: Board of Deputies of British Jews declares Greens to be racist party
description: The Green Party of England and Wales has been declared a racist organisation by the Board of Deputies of British Jews.The Jewish body, which is the la
body: The Green Party of England and Wales has been declared a racist organisation by the Board of Deputies of British Jews.The Jewish body, which is the largest in the UK, was responding to the "Zionism is racism" policy motion passed at the Green Party's conference earlier this month.Board of Deputies president Phil Rosenberg said a vote passed by 118 votes to one to declare that the Greens had, "by adopting an antisemitic platform, become a racist party".A spokesman for the Greens insisted the party does not discriminate against people who hold Zionist views and said it rejected the Board of Deputies' "characterisation of this motion and our party".They added the decision "will not stop us from speaking out against the genocide in Gaza and pushing for stronger sanctions against the Israeli government and its leaders". Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.The motion passed by the Board of Deputies, external urged other parties not to do deals with the Greens unless they rejected the policy.Forming coalition deals with Greens at local or national level would be "failing to take antisemitism with the requisite seriousness", it said, unless the party's local leadership have rejected the policy and committed to overturn it.Labour has already issued an ultimatum to local Green groups it is currently in coalition with, telling them to disown the motion or lose the party's support.Rosenberg said: "By adopting an antisemitic platform, the Green Party of England and Wales has become a racist party. We will treat it accordingly."No political party has the right to tell Jews that a central part of our identity, rooted in thousands of years of history, faith and peoplehood, is racist."The Green Party's policy brands much of our community, including our synagogues and communal organisations, with that slur. It gives prejudice against Jews a political licence."The Green Party's leadership must now take responsibility for reversing this policy and confronting the antisemitism it has legitimised."The motion backed by Green members at its party conference earlier this month said Zionism was an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/ or domination of the non-Jewish population".It was criticised by Jewish groups, as well as four Green MPs and two former leaders, and opposition political parties. Responding when the Green motion was passed, the Board of Deputies and Jewish Leadership Council said in a joint statement that "Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it".Green Party leader Zack Polanski, who is Jewish, did not take part in the vote on the motion as he left the conference early to campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election which was held days later.He has since told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that, while he would like to make amendments, he would not overturn the motion, which would be party policy until 2028.

schema.headline: Board of Deputies of British Jews declares Greens to be racist party

title: Meghan broke contact with father in letter citing abuse claims
description: The Duchess of Sussex broke contact with her father last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls, the BBC understands
body: The Duchess of Sussex broke contact with her father last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls, the BBC understands.Sources close to the duchess said Meghan warned Thomas Markle in a letter that he would never meet his grandchildren.It is understood the letter was sent to Markle, 82, while he was in hospital in the Philippines after having his leg amputated.It has been reported that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Markle had been found in his former home in the Philippines and UK police in 2019 told Meghan about claims of abuse against him. Markle, who is based in the US, denies all such allegations. Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018. He pulled out of his daughter's royal wedding that year, citing ill health.The letter sent in 2025 appears to be the end of what has been a troubled relationship between father and daughter.It is understood details of the letter, first reported in the Sun on Sunday, external, include Meghan telling Markle that he would never meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lillibet, with Meghan making it clear she would never contact her father again.She also apparently told her father that authorities were aware of the claims made against him.Meghan's half-brother Thomas Markle Jnr claimed to the Sun on Friday he found a stash of images belonging to his father at his former Philippines home.He is said to have told police he discovered child abuse videos and pictures among the items. He is understood to have contacted the US Federal Bureau of Investigations (FBI) about it in July.The FBI has since confirmed it is aware of the allegations.On Sunday Markle Jnr, 60, apologised to Meghan in an interview with the Sun for initially siding with her father during their long-running estrangement."I now know I have been protecting the wrong person for the past nine years," he said.Philippines officials have confirmed they are investigating the allegations about Meghan's father, telling the BBC on Friday that its anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force was investigating the matter.Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately said national police had secured Thomas Markle's computer and would carry out a digital forensic examination.Meanwhile, Thomas Markle has given an interview to the Mail on Sunday, external in which he acknowledged paying for sex in the Philippines on past visits but denies sleeping with underage girls and ever possessing child abuse images.

schema.headline: Meghan broke contact with father in letter citing abuse claims

title: Opposition leader María Machado returns to Venezuela
description: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado has returned home to a fraught political landscape after more than 10 months in exile."I am here. Wi
body: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado has returned home to a fraught political landscape after more than 10 months in exile."I am here. With you," Machado wrote on X on Sunday. Her return comes after repeated prior efforts to re-enter came to no avail. In January, a month after Machado left Venezuela on a speedboat under cover of darkness to accept the Nobel Peace Prize in Norway, the US seized her opponent, President Nicolás Maduro. The Trump administration then backed his deputy, Delcy Rodríguez, as leader and she was sworn in as interim president, later signing an oil deal which granted very favourable terms to the US.Machado was photographed on Sunday attending Mass at a church in the Venezuelan state of Lara, surrounded by supporters hugging her and clasping her hands. Her ally, former presidential candidate Edmundo González, confirmed her arrival, writing in a statement: "I am thrilled to announce to you that our leader, my dear María Corina, is on Venezuelan soil.""Today is a very important day for Venezuelans. Our sovereign voice returns with her to lead and guide this process!" González said.He added that he will soon join Machado in Venezuela to advance the country "toward freedom".An advisor to Machado said in September that over the previous few weeks Machado had attempted seven times to return to Venezuela, but was denied each time. There have been reports that the US was involved in delaying her return, which it has denied. It's unclear what Machado plans to do next now that she's back, but she has previously said she would run for president again if an election were held. Her ability to return to her country was always contingent on approval from the Trump administration, which it appears has now been granted.A staunch supporter of democracy, Machado won an independent presidential primary election - held outside the Maduro government's official election authority - in 2023, earning more than 90% of the vote.Despite winning the primary, Maduro's government barred Machado from running for office, accusing her of fraud and tax violations. Machado denied the allegations, calling them politically motivated. She spent her final days in the country hiding in safehouses before her fleeing to Norway to accept the Nobel Prize.In the 2024 election, Machado's ally González ran in her place against Maduro.The electoral authority, which is closely aligned with the government, declared Maduro the winner without making detailed voting tallies public.The opposition argued that González won the election, not Maduro, uploading copies of the voting tallies as evidence.Maduro was removed from the country by US forces in January, and is currently jailed in New York where he faces drugs, weapons and torture charges. He has pleaded not guilty. A spokesman for Machado called her return "a major step toward a democratic transition and free, fair, and verifiable presidential elections in the near future"."We thank President Donald Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the US Government, Congress, and allied governments for their continued leadership and support," her spokesperson, David Smolansky, added.Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump said, "I don't know anything about" her return, and added that he hoped she was "safe". "I think she's a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel Prize, so how can I say anything else? And I hope she's safe," he said.In January, Machado visited the White House and gifted her Nobel prize award to Trump. The committee that issues the prize had said "it cannot be revoked, shared, or transferred to others".US Secretary of State Marco Rubio praised his country's role in securing her return through political reconciliation talks. "The conditions allowing for the safe return of Ms Machado to Venezuela is the direct result of the US supported reconciliation talks which has already seen hundreds of political prisoners freed and hundreds of political opposition figures return from exile," he posted on X.He added: "We expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in thirty years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election but an enduring democracy."

schema.headline: Opposition leader María Machado returns to Venezuela

title: Suspect in deadly Paris suburb shooting sent for psychiatric observation
description: The lawyer for Pengo Bossio Wangi, the one person killed during the attack, told French media the move to place the suspect under observation was "ver
body: The lawyer for Pengo Bossio Wangi, the one person killed during the attack, told French media the move to place the suspect under observation was "very rare".He alleged that it was being used to portray the suspect as criminally irresponsible rather than having acted deliberately.Wangi, a 26-year-old French-Congolese martial artist, was named as the one fatality on Saturday.The mixed martial arts club where he trained paid tribute to him, saying: "On the mats as off them, he was one of those who lead by example: present, respectful, always ready to lift others up. "His smile, his energy and his generosity will remain etched in our walls and in our hearts."Three of those injured in the attack were taken to hospital in a serious condition - including a 12-year-old girl who remains in a critical condition.The mayor of La Verrière, Nicolas Dainville, told French radio network France Info on Sunday that he had spoken to the girl's mother over the phone and confirmed she was "doing better".Another injured resident was recovering while a third remained in a critical condition, he said.The suspect had been known to police prior to the attack but not to France's intelligence services, local media report. PNAT previously said he had four previous convictions that had been "automatically expunged".He is thought to have used an old semi-automatic weapon during the attack, firing in bursts from his car window.

schema.headline: Suspect in deadly Paris suburb shooting sent for psychiatric observation

title: Pakistan vs England: Shadab Khan condemns Harry Brook's side to another improbable loss
description: One-day international tri-series, LahoreEngland 241 (46.4 overs): Duckett 105 (111), Shaheen 4-46Pakistan 243-9 (47.1 overs): Shadab 113* (96), Overto
body: One-day international tri-series, LahoreEngland 241 (46.4 overs): Duckett 105 (111), Shaheen 4-46Pakistan 243-9 (47.1 overs): Shadab 113* (96), Overton 3-43Pakistan won by one wicketScorecardEngland somehow lost another one-day international from a seemingly unbeatable position thanks to an improbable last-wicket stand by Pakistan in Lahore.Three days after conceding 430 to lose to Sri Lanka, Harry Brook's side were beaten despite reducing Pakistan to 154-9 in pursuit of 242.Shadab Khan was the engineer of Pakistan's unlikely win, striking a quite brilliant unbeaten 113 - the highest score by a number eight in an ODI.He was supported by Haris Rauf, Pakistan's number 11 contributing seven to the unbroken 10th-wicket partnership of 89 - comfortably a new record for a last-wicket pair to win an ODI.In barely believable scenes, Shadab was given out lbw to Gus Atkinson on 97, with 21 runs still required.The players shook hands before Shadab called for a speculative review. DRS found a tiny inside edge and, reprieved, he watched Rauf belt debutant Henry Crocombe down the ground for the winning boundary with 17 balls to spare.It means England are all but out of the tri-series - their exit will be confirmed if Sri Lanka beat Pakistan on Tuesday.A second implosion in as many matches is hugely concerning for England, who looked to be on course for victory despite being bowled out for only 241.Ben Duckett made a fine 105 - only the opener, Sam Curran and Gus Atkinson passing 20 in blameless conditions.Nevertheless, England were well on course thanks to a collectively relentless display from their bowlers. Jamie Overton bowled his 10 overs in one spell for 3-43.Then came Shadab and another baffling defeat for England, who could be out before they play their final game against Sri Lanka on Thursday.With less than a year to go to the World Cup, this tri-series was designed to give England experience of the pressure and permutations of tournament play.In a matter of days, they have gone through two extreme situations, both ending in crushing defeats. What linked both matches was England's powerlessness to salvage the situation once the momentum turned against them.If anything, the finish to this match was more dramatic than Sri Lanka pulling off the second-highest chase in ODI history.Even Shadab was convinced he was out when he was hit on the shin by Atkinson's low full toss - he called for the hopeful review as he was walking off the field. When it came back in his favour, he put his head in his hands and was embraced by Rauf.In the heat of the tight finish, Rauf had to be pulled away from a confrontation with England's Will Jacks when a Sam Curran bouncer was not called wide, while Rauf could also have been run out by Tom Banton's flick from mid-on when 18 were still required.Shadab expertly farmed the strike - Rauf faced only 19 deliveries in a stand that lasted 80 balls.Rauf defended his first 18 balls then cut loose to his 19th, hammering Crocombe for four then running away and throwing his bat in the air to begin the joyous celebrations.What must England do to win a match in this tri-series? They have lost all three of their matches, the past two in extraordinary circumstances.Yes, England are without key players Jofra Archer, Jos Buttler and Jacob Bethell on this tour, while Adil Rashid has been omitted from the XI and Josh Tongue missed out with a toe injury. Still, what they are learning is they do not respond well in tight situations. On Thursday, the batters broke records, only to be let down by the bowlers. On Sunday, the bowlers were on course to mask the deficiencies of the batters, then wilted when it mattered.This loss means encouraging performances from Duckett and Overton will be forgotten. For Duckett, this was a much-needed score at time when questions have been asked about his position. Overton was superb, the first England seamer to bowl 10 consecutive overs in an ODI since 2017.But, when England needed inspiration to take the last wicket, they were found wanting. Maybe the pace of Archer or Tongue, or mystery of Rashid would have made the difference.They crowded the bat for Rauf, tried to defend against Shadab and held countless meetings. Heads dropped, plans failed and England were not good enough.To focus only on England does a disservice to Shadab, who played a knock for the ages, one of the greatest by a Pakistan batter in an ODI.The all-rounder had been left out of the first two matches of this series. After bowling seven overs with his leg-spin, he arrived to bat when his team were in disarray at 103-6, then left as a hero.Shadab was unflappable in the face of such a monumental task, supported by the fiery Rauf. In a 96-ball stay, Shadab expertly picked his moments to attack, pouncing when England erred. He hit five sixes and 13 fours.Rauf batted for 70 minutes, more than two times his previous longest stay in an ODI. Only once before had he faced more deliveries.As tension rose, so did the tempers - Joe Root had to step in to guide Rauf away from Jacks.Rauf had the last word, but this will be remembered as Shadab's match.

schema.headline: Pakistan vs England: Shadab Khan condemns Harry Brook's side to another improbable loss

title: Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement
description: The prime minister says he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and European Union.Spe
body: The prime minister says he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and European Union.Speaking to the Sunday Times, Andy Burnham said a new relationship with Brussels could include full EU membership or joining the single market, requiring free movement.Asked about Burnham's remarks, Angela Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg "you can't take anything off the table", adding the prime minister was saying "we've got to be pragmatic to get the best deal for Britain and he wants to have the conversation." Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch responded that the prime minister "hasn't thought this through", while Reform UK's Robert Jenrick dismissed the idea as "mad".Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the Leave campaign raising issues about rules allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.Burnham has previously committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto which ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.He has said that any changes would require a mandate at a general election, would is due by 2029."I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this," he told the Sunday Times, external, adding he believed the type of migration had changed from revolving door movement of young people."Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different," he said. "The balance of migration has changed, hasn't it, since then? I think we've just got to have an honest discussion about those things."But he stressed: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."The Schengen Agreement allows passport-free travel across EU countries. The UK was able to keep the pound when it was an EU member, but the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the Euro.His remarks were made ahead of an EU summit on 20 November in Brussels, where the prime minister is expected to pitch options for a reset of relations with the bloc.On Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Rayner said she wanted to see the best possible deal with the European Union, which may well involve concessions."What the prime minister is saying now, and what I want, is that we have an honest conversation about the facts of what the trade-offs are to get the best deal for Britain going forward," she said."The frustration for me in the previous debate we had when we had the referendum is that a lot of those facts didn't get the airtime... So I would like us to have an honest conversation about what the trade-offs could be and then put that to the people at a general election."Writing on X, Badenoch dismissed it as "yet another example of Burnham's foot in mouth syndrome".She added: "Most people who voted for Brexit did so because they didn't want free movement. Too many politicians have failed to understand the significance and impact of immigration on communities."Conservative MP and former chancellor Jeremy Hunt, who backed Remain, warned the Brexit debate was "incredibly divisive" and insisted the current Brexit deal can still be made to work."I was at the top of a government that was paralysed for several years while we were trying to wrestle with the implications of that vote and I think, having made the decision, we should stick with it and make the most of it - I think we can make it a success," he told Kuenssberg.Pointing to the one million young people not in work or training, he added: "Surely our priority in that situation is to get those jobs filled by the young people we have here instead of parking them on welfare."Which is why I think it's astonishing to lead on the issue of free movement... Something that is actually going to stop young people here getting jobs."But Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper told Kuenssberg she believed allowing freedom of movement would be "a really good thing for growth" and pushed for the UK to rejoin the single market, the customs union, and also be involved in the bloc's defence pact. The UK currently has "the worst of both worlds" on immigration, she said, as it was excluded from the EU's "new asylum pact with biometric data" that could be used to "tackle the small boats crisis".Reform UK's economy spokesperson Robert Jenrick told Kuenssberg he had never believed freedom of movement "was a good thing", despite supporting the Remain position before the 2016 referendum when he was a Conservative MP."I think it's completely mad, the idea that this country needs more immigration," he said, claiming data shows mass migration "has been a disaster for working people, for Brits"."The last thing they want is their wages being undercut by a load of low wage, low-skilled migrants from overseas," he added.

schema.headline: Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement

title: Donegal: Brown bears adjusting to new life in Irish countryside
description: From Russian cages to Irish sanctuary: The five-year rescue journey of Bu and TyapaImage source, Wild Ireland press handoutImage caption, Tyapa (left)
body: From Russian cages to Irish sanctuary: The five-year rescue journey of Bu and TyapaImage source, Wild Ireland press handoutImage caption, Tyapa (left) and Bu (right) were previously kept in small cages in the Republic of Dagestan in RussiaByMike McBrideBBC News NIAfter years in cramped cages, two brown bears are adjusting to their new life following a remarkable rescue mission that spanned multiple countries, was disrupted by two major conflicts and involved more than 100 people.For Bu and Tyapa, the five-year rescue journey from the Republic of Dagestan in Russia to the Irish countryside was anything but straightforward.One bear had spent their life forced to perform in a circus, while the other was confined to a cage so small they could not stand upright.Today, the bears are now adjusting to a totally different world among the trees and grass at Wild Ireland, a sanctuary for rescued animals in County Donegal.Image caption, Tyapa is slowly settling into her new surroundings in Burnfoot, County DonegalWild Ireland founder Killian McLaughlin first learned about Bu and Tyapa in 2021 and committed to bringing them to safety in Donegal.The sanctuary, located in Burnfoot, opened in October 2019 and provides a safe space for animals, including brown bears, monkeys, wolves, and lynx.Image caption, Wild Ireland founder Killian McLaughlin says the bears' health improvements since their arrival have been remarkableMcLaughlin said the two bears were in extremely poor health when they were first rescued.Former circus bear Bu had spent years confined to a small indoor cage after being forced to perform.McLaughlin said Tyapa had lived in a cage measuring just 2.5m by 2.5m by 2m, which was too low for him to stand upright and had no roof, which left him exposed to the harsh winters and blistering summer heat.The bear had no water dish and relied on a hose for drinking water. McLaughlin said he was being raised to be killed for an eventual taxidermy display.When the bears were rescued, both were severely malnourished and showed signs of psychological trauma.Blood tests also revealed serious kidney problems associated with prolonged dehydration.How do you transport two large bears?Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 made the original transport route through Ukraine impossible, said McLaughlin.An alternative route through the Middle East was then explored, but plans were disrupted again in February 2026 when the escalating conflict involving Iran led to airspace closures and flight disruptions across the region.More than 100 people were involved in the rescue operation, including volunteers, lawyers, veterinarians, animal transport specialists, cargo teams and officials in Russia, the United Arab Emirates and Ireland.Image source, Wild Ireland press handoutImage caption, The bears travelled from Moscow via Abu Dhabi to Dublin, arriving in the Republic of Ireland on 3 August 2026In late October 2025, Dima and Yana Kim, who work at Tiger House, a sanctuary near St Petersburg that cares for former circus tigers, embarked on a 36-hour drive to Dagestan to rescue the bears.Bu and Tyapa had to be cut out of their rusting steel cages, sedated and placed in secure transport crates for the journey back to Tiger House, where they received veterinary treatment and underwent quarantine.After months of preparation and repeated delays, the bears eventually travelled from Moscow via Abu Dhabi to Dublin, arriving in Ireland in August.Health improvements since arrivingSince arriving at Wild Ireland, McLaughlin said both bears have gained weight, their coats have improved, and follow-up blood tests have shown that their kidney function has returned to normal.He said their habitat provides woodland, water and room to explore, as well as sheltered areas where they can retreat or move out of public view if they would like some privacy."These bears have suffered trauma and the first step of that recovery process is get them back out into the forest, get their paws into the soil and on the grass and get them exploring."We hope they can now have a full and happy life."Working with bears isn't your normal 9-5Working with bears is certainly not your everyday job, but for Wild Ireland team member Chloe McElhatton, it's one she absolutely relishes.Chloe has been working at Wild Ireland for just over a year. She studied zoology at Queen's University Belfast, completing a four-year degree before joining the team."This is obviously a very unique job, and it's quite different from what most people would do," she said. Image caption, Chloe McElhatton is part of the bear team at Wild Ireland and says looking after bears is not your average 9-5 job"We've done a lot of work hiding food around the bear habitats, encouraging them to search and forage for it themselves and this promotes their natural behaviours and helps them become more comfortable in that new open space," she said."Over time, we've seen their confidence build, and you can see great changes, both physically and mentally, in both of them."What do visitors think of the bears?Image caption, Liam, who is from France, says the two bears are big and impressiveLiam, who is from France, said the bears were one of his favourite animals to see when visiting the park."Very big and very impressive," is how he summed up Bu and Tyapa."I saw chickens, some wolves and some monkeys and then the bears which were definitely my favourite."Image caption, Chris Roberts is a regular visitor to Wild Ireland and came to visit hoping to see a glimpse of the two new bears Chris Roberts is from Manorcunningham, about 20 minutes from Wild Ireland, and has been visiting the site ever since it first opened in 2019."I've lost count of how many times we've been here, but we really wanted to come down today to see if we could catch a glimpse of Bu and Tyapa."It was fantastic to see them in the flesh."We absolutely loved it and are delighted to see them doing so well, especially considering their backstory and the awful conditions they were once kept in."

schema.headline: Donegal: Brown bears adjusting to new life in Irish countryside

title: Musk says SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink connection as service restored
description: Elon Musk has said his company SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink internet service, after Ukrainian officials said connectivity issues appeared to h
body: Elon Musk has said his company SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink internet service, after Ukrainian officials said connectivity issues appeared to have been resolved.The tech billionaire accused Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using it for military activity - but denied being responsible for a simultaneous issue with its US-run, military-grade counterpart Starshield.Kyiv has not officially commented on Musk's latest claim but Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said his post was "very strange".Musk had earlier denied deliberately throttling Ukraine's connection, which it says hampered its ability to conduct defensive operations for more than a week.The issue first emerged last week during a broader row between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.Musk's latest comments, and the seeming restoration of the service, came after US President Donald Trump said he had told the Tesla and X owner to "put it back", having repeatedly denied instructing him to limit the service."Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote on X on Saturday. "Ukraine['s] military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."He went on to say that SpaceX had "done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth" and reiterated his stipulation that Starshield was a different system and controlled by the US government, adding: "What they decide to do is up to them."He added in a later post: "[Starlink] can be used for infrastructure that is military, but it cannot be used for unequivocally offensive strikes that make it fair game to be struck back."Reacting to Musk's post, Beskrestnov said that drones operating via Starlink in Ukraine had a speed restriction of 70-90km/h (43-56mph) and did not work on Russian territory."Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and medium-range strikes," he wrote on Telegram."It is very strange that Elon Musk is not aware of Starlink restrictions in Ukraine."There was no immediate comment from Ukraine's defence ministry.Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed, both of which run on networks of low Earth orbit satellites launched by SpaceX.Starlink allows military units to co-ordinate, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield, while Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones.Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.Ukraine's Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said earlier on Saturday that the military was now recording a "stable connection", with drones now able to reach speeds in excess of 400km/h. Kyiv previously said the connection would cut out above 161km/h."The speeds are now where they need to be," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram. Musk did not disclose in his post why SpaceX had chosen to make the change to its service last week, when Ukraine's extensive use of Starlink had been known for several years.The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic standoff between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war.Faced with midterm elections next month and domestic displeasure with rising fuel prices, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal with Moscow - criticised by European allies as funding Russia's war machine - to supply Russian diesel to the US and the global market.Zelensky initially agreed to cease strikes targeting Russian oil facilities on the proviso that Moscow cease striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, before restarting the strikes after several instances of Russia disregarding this.The Ukrainian leader said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied.Fighting and aerial attacks continued to be exchanged between Russia and Ukraine overnight.Ukraine's emergency services said three people were killed and 15 others injured, including an 11-year-old girl, in attacks on the Dnipropetrovsk region, in the south east.Another six people were injured when a Russian drone struck an apartment block in the central city of Vinnytsia, it said.The Russian defence ministry said on Sunday that it had struck a cargo vessel it claimed was being used to supply the Ukrainian army while it was en route to the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk overnight.It also said Russian forces hit a logistics centre, a distribution centre and a logistics terminal in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv.Ukraine's defence ministry earlier said it struck a facility in the Russian city of Oryol run by a sanctioned heavy machinery manufacturer. Russian authorities said three people were killed in the strike. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, with fighting now into its fifth year.

schema.headline: Musk says SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink connection as service restored

title: Manchester United - Michael Carrick future as manager under major threat
description: Michael Carrick's future as Manchester United manager is under major threat following the home loss to Bournemouth on Sunday.The Red Devils lost 3-0 a
body: Michael Carrick's future as Manchester United manager is under major threat following the home loss to Bournemouth on Sunday.The Red Devils lost 3-0 as their poor start to the season continued - they have won just one of their eight Premier League matches so far and sit 16th - 14 points off the top.Carrick, 45, took interim charge in January following Ruben Amorim's departure and he was rewarded with the permanent job in May after securing Champions League qualification with an impressive run that resulted in them finishing third.But United have not won in the top flight since 30 August, when they defeated newly promoted Ipswich 5-2."See what happens," Carrick told BBC Sport when asked if he was expecting any conversations on his future. "I'm not expecting anything. It's just digesting today - we knew it was an important day to try and get us moving forward and we haven't done that. "For me it's just digesting that and the emotions at the end of the game is something I've not really had before."Carrick made a big call on Sunday by dropping his captain Bruno Fernandes to the bench.That decision came after the Portugal midfielder questioned Carrick's tactics in Wednesday's 4-1 loss at Como in the Champions League.The comments from Fernandes came in the wake of defender Lisandro Martinez issuing an apology following his controversial remarks criticising the club's hierarchy.Martinez said he had expected more investment in the Manchester United squad and "more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox]".Carrick made 464 appearances for Manchester United in a playing career at the club that spanned 12 years.As a consequence, he remains a popular figure among the fans, who chanted his song at full-time in the loss to Bournemouth as he did a lap of the pitch to applaud the supporters."It wasn't a farewell from me," Carrick said on Sky Sports."I've mixed emotions, I'm feeling it for my players, they're going through a tough spell. Some of it we can help, some of it the situation unravels and the boys are feeling it at the moment. "Mixed emotions for the supporters to respond in that way. To have that connection with the supporters it's mixed emotions, it'll take a bit of time to digest but I certainly appreciate their support."The situation is where we are and we haven't had results or performances that have been good enough."Former Manchester United defender Gary Neville said on Sky Sports: "The Manchester United fans are singing the Michael Carrick song because I think they know what's going to happen here. They've seen this before. He's one of their own and he's popular."But the owners, the sporting department and the players are not popular and they've badly let this football club down."Those two [Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox] tomorrow are probably going to make a decision that will disgust Manchester United fans, but it's probably necessary."It's just an absolute mess."Those chants in support of Carrick turned to boos after he had left the pitch as supporters appeared to show their frustration with the club's players and hierarchy. "That says everything to me," former Premier League striker Clinton Morrison said. "They're with Carrick the fans but they're not with the players. Wow. That was alarming."Carrick got a big cheer but as soon it was just the players, they got booed. But they've not been good enough and they deserve to get booed. There's only so much a manager can do."The players are not good enough, in my opinion, to win football matches."Ex-Manchester United full-back Ashley Young added: "Unfortunately for Michael Carrick, it's so disappointing. "The fans are behind him and backing him and of course they are, because he's a legend of the football club. But the players on the pitch showed nothing. They didn't run, they didn't look like a team together."If you looked at the difference to the Bournemouth team, you'd swap every single player for that Manchester United team. It was a poor showing."With Fernandes on the bench against Bournemouth, Harry Maguire was given the captain's armband for the day.The defender insisted after the game that Carrick has the full support of the dressing room."We're fully behind Michael [Carrick]," Maguire told BBC Sport."Coming into the team last season he turned things around and got Champions League football this season. "As individuals, we're not playing well enough."Carrick has won just two Premier League matches since he was given the job on a permanent basis."When you play for this club you know you're two or three games away from that happening," Maguire said of Manchester United's downturn in form."You have to find something within yourself to help the club, help the team and get out of this. "We will start winning football matches but we have to do it quickly."

schema.headline: Manchester United - Michael Carrick future as manager under major threat

title: Music streaming: Why we're listening to so many old songs
description: Why the charts are full of old songs - and so are your playlistsImage source, Getty Images for iHeartRadioImage caption, One of 2026's biggest hits is
body: Why the charts are full of old songs - and so are your playlistsImage source, Getty Images for iHeartRadioImage caption, One of 2026's biggest hits is Zara Larsson's Lush Life, originally released in 2015ByThomas SpencerMore music is being created than at any other time in human history. Every day, more than 100,000 songs, external are being submitted to streaming services. And despite the deluge of AI music, external - Spotify says it has removed 75 million "spammy tracks" from its catalogue - real music still makes up most of our listening. The streaming service Deezer says AI accounts for just 0.5% of streams on its platform.The problem for all those artists creating new music is that our listening habits increasingly show a love for nostalgia.Luminate, an independent entertainment data and analytics company that tracks music, film, and television consumption first started tracking music streaming in 2008.This year, it recorded that the streaming of current music (released less than 18 months ago) was significantly dwarfed by older music in both the UK and US.In the first half of 2026, almost two thirds of the music played (about 60%) was released five or more years ago.So, if we're stuck in a streaming rut, what's to blame?Old vs new?In the UK, most of us seem to be shunning new songs.Eighteen of the year's top 20 bestselling songs, external were released 12 months ago, or earlier. The year's eighth biggest hit is Zara Larsson's Lush Life, which originally came out in June 2015. Michael Jackson's Billie Jean (1983) is in 22nd place. Fleetwood Mac's Dreams (1977) is 30th.It's a sign that, with practically every song ever recorded available at the press of a button, people are increasingly seeking out the classics - or what the music industry categorises as "deep catalogue".It's a similar story in the US.There, in the two most-played genres, R&B and Hip-Hop, external, about 60% of streams are old-school catalogue hits.A 'drought' of new music in the UK Charts?Even when current songs do break out, they themselves dominate streaming for weeks and even months.Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's duet Rein Me In recently made UK chart history, spending a record-breaking 23 non-consecutive weeks at number one.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Olivia Dean and Sam Fender have broken chart history with Rein Me In, after 19 non-consecutive weeks at the top of the UK singles chartWhat about grassroots music?Even after a song has gone viral, some musicians say it can be hard to promote subsequent releases and sustain a career. A platform like TikTok isn't set up to boost artists, it's there to create viral moments around a single song."It's easier [today] for folks to be passive fans," noted J Erving, the founder of Raye's distribution company, Human Re Sources, in a recent interview with Billboard, external. "For you to consider yourself broken [as a mainstream artist], people need to care about you beyond the song. Where is the connectivity? Are people really dialled in in a deeper way?" It's a problem the music industry is keen to tackle.Oliver Schusser, the Head of Apple Music, says his streaming service is working to champion "tomorrow's artists" in its curation."You know, we do the Super Bowl halftime show, we need to make sure that we still have performers in 10, 20, 30 years," he tells BBC News. "Because if you look back at the performers we had in the last four years, they all started somewhere before they got to the world's biggest stage."Other organisations like Sofar Sounds work exclusively with grassroots musicians, putting on intimate pop-up gigs in cities across the globe.This October, its Shoreditch Sofar Fringe festival showcased a whole host of artists like East London rapper J Casa.Image source, J CasaImage caption, Rapper J Casa is one of thousands of grassroots artists trying to cut through the noise on streaming platformsIn an age of content oversaturation, Casa thinks there's something unique about a live performance.Rather than hearing more of what they already know, Casa says audiences form "a lasting connection" with a new artist and their music.Sofar is also launching its Human Discovery Movement, external campaign that aims to put music curation and discovery "back into human hands."Music lovers can now text a "mystery number" and receive voice notes from Sofar's tastemakers with recommendations for new music worldwide.Are streaming platforms preaching to the choir?Artificial intelligence (AI) may also be playing its part in the so-called death of new music.Spotify, and its competitors like Apple Music and Amazon Music, are driving the trend in AI-assisted curation, allowing premium subscribers to automatically generate playlists through text prompts to fit a mood, vibe or occasion.Musicologist Anna-Kaisa Kaila thinks "there absolutely is potential for bias" with AI-generative playlist technology."With AI systems, the bias can either come from the data or from the system itself. If there's not enough training data in a particular style that is perhaps not so commercially dominant, it will be that much harder for the system to pull up tracks in that style."Others fear an algorithmic streaming bubble is to the detriment of genuine music, its discovery and creatives' livelihoods.As Tim Garcia, London-based DJ and curator puts it: "They're based on everyone's listening behaviour and data, right? So, you're probably going to get given a very similar recommendation to an artist you're already listening to."Dan Mackta, managing director at Qobuz, an online music platform that maintains a strict human-first approach to curation, agrees the technology "is never going to want to throw a curve ball at you".Image source, Jordan MatykaImage caption, London-based artist Chiminyo performs at his ongoing jazz-electronic NRG projectChiminyo, a London-based independent artist, believes that auto-generated playlists are also misleading people into thinking they're listening to "hand-picked" tunes from bona fide artists - as opposed to digitally mass-produced sound-alikes created to catch streams.Scrolling through a "relaxing jazz piano playlist" with over 370,000 saves on Spotify, he spots that top featured artists that rack up hundreds of thousands of monthly listens have unverified accounts.Little - if anything - can be found about them online, he says.To his trained ear, Chiminyo also says the different artists' tracks sound near identical, reason enough to conclude the compositions have been synthetically mass-produced."Its all the same: the same piano feel, the same microphone placement, the same tape machine, has been used on every single one of these tracks."When asked, Spotify said it had rolled out platform-wide policies, external against impersonation and is working to the improve filtering out of AI-related issues on its platform. But it acknowledges AI's use in music production sits on a spectrum with some artists choosing to use it to varying degrees.New music may not be dying out, but it's clear it has a lot to contend with in 2026.

schema.headline: Music streaming: Why we're listening to so many old songs

title: Four ways Labour could raise money in the Budget without hiking income tax
description: ByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondentWe're likely to hear a lot about the chancellor's "headroom" in this Budget.That is the cash buffer the gove
body: ByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondentWe're likely to hear a lot about the chancellor's "headroom" in this Budget.That is the cash buffer the government has to help meet its own fiscal rules and reduce borrowing.Economists think the buffer might have halved in the last six months from around £24bn to as low as £11bn, in part because of rising interest rates the government has been paying to borrow money from private investors.The Chancellor, John Healey, might need to raise money to restore it, which would show the government's plan to reduce borrowing by the end of this Parliament is still on track.At the same time, he is under pressure to find money to help people with the rising cost of living and to fund spending on defence. However, Labour's 2024 election manifesto pledged not to raise the rates of income tax, VAT or National Insurance.Increasing taxes on capital gains or extending the mansion tax had been raised as possible options but have since been ruled out by government sources.BBC Verify has looked at what other options could be on the table for the chancellor to raise some more money, external on Wednesday.1. Increase taxes on banksBanks in the UK have seen profits rise in recent years because they have been able to charge people higher interest rates when borrowing money.And there is widespread belief among bank bosses that the chancellor is preparing to raise taxes on banks in this week's Budget.Think tank Tax Policy Associates estimates, external that increasing the surcharge that banks pay on corporation tax from 3% to 5.5% could potentially raise an additional £1bn to £2bn a year for the Treasury.2. Higher taxes on gambling machinesFormer Prime Minister Gordon Brown has called on Healey to hike the tax on electronic gaming machines - such as those found in betting shops and adult gaming centres which can offer payouts of £500 per game - citing the social harm imposed by problem gambling.The Social Market Foundation (SMF) think tank has estimated, external that doubling tax on these machines from 20% to 40% could raise could raise between £275m and £460m - depending on how gamblers reacted to it.People who use gambling machines could also end up having the tax passed on to them through worse odds on games, though anti-gambling groups argue this could help discourage more people from using them.Research from the SMF found that gambling machines are increasingly clustered on some of the UK's most deprived high streets, and that one in four people who play casino games on these machines gamble at risky or harmful levels.3. Get online marketplaces to collect VATReports suggest the chancellor is preparing to announce that big online marketplaces such as Amazon, Ebay and Temu will be made responsible for collecting tax owed by retailers selling on their platforms.The Treasury estimates it is missing out on around £12bn a year, external in VAT revenues that should be paid by companies, which it calls the "VAT tax gap".Tax experts say that part of the problem - although not accounting for the full £12bn of the VAT gap - is that some online sellers fail to comply with VAT rules, either by not charging VAT when they should or by failing to pass on VAT collected from customers to the government.Enforcement can be difficult because some firms that use platforms like Amazon to sell their products are based overseas and falsely present themselves as UK-established businesses.Others close down and reopen under different company names to escape their tax liabilities.Reports suggest that this move to make big online marketplaces responsible for collecting the tax - rather than the individual retailers - would clamp down on this form of tax evasion and could raise around £1bn in extra VAT a year.Amazon, which supports the move, has estimated it could raise £700m, external a year in VAT for the government.Some sellers could respond by raising prices or leaving the platform, which could have an impact on some shoppers.However, it would also level the playing field for online sellers, ensuring those businesses who charge VAT are not illegally undercut by those who break the rules and do not.4. Cut welfare spendingThe above three tax measures together would raise a maximum of only around £3.5bn a year.That would be small relative to the sums of money the chancellor might well need to restore his headroom and pay for any new spending.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in the summer he wanted a "fair and lasting" reduction to the UK's welfare bill, while the government is under pressure from opposition parties to find savings from working-age benefits.The Conservatives claim they could make savings of £36bn a year by restricting people's access to welfare payments.Reform say they would save £50bn a year in this way, although independent analysts say there are questions about how realistic it is to make such large savings.Working health and sickness benefits have risen sharply since the Covid pandemic and the overall cost is projected by the Office for Budget Responsibility to increase from £68bn this year to £81bn in 2031.Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves attempted to reduce spending on these benefits , externalby £5bn a year by 2030, but were forced to reverse course after a revolt by backbench Labour MPs.Independent welfare experts and economists say savings from the working age welfare budget are possible but would likely require upfront spending to help people into work, which could cancel out any near-term savings for the Treasury.Cuts to health and disability welfare would reduce the incomes of people who currently receive those payments, external and/or those who would otherwise receive them in future - and campaigners warn of the risk of people being pushed into poverty.However, if more welfare claimants were also supported into work, their overall incomes could be maintained or even rise.Graphics by Callum Thomson and Lewis McBlane.Get in touchWhat are you hoping for from the Budget? What questions do you have?

schema.headline: Four ways Labour could raise money in the Budget without hiking income tax

title: The penguins are noisy, the people fantastic - what it takes to be an Antarctic postmaster
description: Image source, UK Antarctic Heritage TrustImage caption, George Clarke is returning for his third stint at Port LockroyByChristopher MaceBristolIt is h
body: Image source, UK Antarctic Heritage TrustImage caption, George Clarke is returning for his third stint at Port LockroyByChristopher MaceBristolIt is hardly a typical round for a postie, but for five months of the year George Clarke leaves behind his partner and friends in Bristol to become a postmaster at the world's most southerly post office - in Antarctica."I thought it sounded like an amazing experience - living away from home for a few months on a very small island with five other people and 1,000 penguins," says Clarke.He takes up his role as Port Lockroy postmaster from late October to March, during the southern hemisphere summer.The part-time festival worker and artist says his days are spent sorting postcards, processing letters and arranging for the post to hitch a ride north on passing ships before being distributed around the world."The penguins are noisy and smelly. The people are fantastic," he said. "I've fallen in love with the Antarctic wilderness."Image source, UKAHTImage caption, Port Lockroy is home to a colony of about 1,000 gentoo penguinsWhen Clarke sets off with in a team of six on Monday, it will be his third voyage to Antarctica helping the UK Antarctic Heritage Trust (UKAHT) to conserve Port Lockroy, a former British science research facility.Unlike a regular post office, there is no fleet of vans ready to whisk the mail away."When we collect up all the postcards and we've sorted through them, we've bagged them up, we've weighed them, we then need to look to see which ships are heading north towards the Falklands," he said."Then we get them on email or the radio and we say, 'Hello, would you mind taking some postcards with you?' And they're always very keen to oblige."Unsurprisingly, running a post office for six people does not take up all of Clarke's time at Port Lockroy.He is also the deputy base commander, helps with the cleaning and maintenance of the site, and helps with wildlife observations for the British Antarctic Survey (BAS)."The primary objective of the charity is conservation of the heritage surrounding UK exploration in Antarctica," Clarke said.Image source, UK Antarctic Heritage TrustImage caption, Postmaster George Clarke says he has fallen in love with the Antarctic wildernessThe team of six is about to embark on the second term of a three-year plan to shore-up and restore the island's largest building, Bransfield House, which is home to a museum, the post office and a shop.They will install beams in the roof and 30 steel and timber props in the floor to help it withstand rain and snow.The site on Goudier Island was chosen in the 1940s to become a permanent British foothold in Antarctica because it was known as a safe place to anchor by early 20th Century whaling ships.The remnants of that industry are still clear to see, with the bones of whales killed long ago for their oil littering part of the shore.Port Lockroy operated until 1962, when British research was moved to larger and more modern sites in Antarctica.Image source, UKAHTImage caption, Clarke (second from left) and the team have been training in the Brecon Beacons before heading to AntarcticaThe journey from the UKAHT base in Cambridgeshire to Port Lockroy takes about a week."We fly to Ushuaia via Buenos Aires in Argentina and we'll probably have a couple of days to acclimatise slightly," Clarke said."We'll then jump on a ship that will take us south to the Antarctic Peninsula and it takes four or five days."Clarke's colleagues are also excited to get the new season under way.Base commander and RAF veteran Carole McCullough said: "I applied for the role looking for a bit of an adventure, and Antarctica is the ultimate adventure."The team work, the bonding, the appreciation of the place - it's all going to make for the most wonderful experience."Wildlife monitor and museum manager Alice Parr added: "I actually applied for a role three years ago and was selected as reserve."I tried again - clearly persistence pays off! I'm incredibly excited to be managing the museum and counting penguins. It's the opportunity of a lifetime."Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: The penguins are noisy, the people fantastic - what it takes to be an Antarctic postmaster

title: Liverpool beat Brighton: Alexander Isak living up to price tag as Liverpool's winning run continues
description: It has been a long time coming but Alexander Isak might finally be living up to his price tag.The Sweden striker arrived at Anfield amid huge fanfare
body: It has been a long time coming but Alexander Isak might finally be living up to his price tag.The Sweden striker arrived at Anfield amid huge fanfare in August 2025 when he signed from Newcastle for a British record £125m.But a combination of a slow start and then suffering a broken leg in December meant his first season at the Reds became something of a nightmare - scoring just four goals in 22 games.This season has been a different story. Isak's goal against Brighton on Sunday helped Liverpool to an impressive 2-0 win against the Premier League's in-form side, taking his tally to six for the campaign already.The 27-year-old is averaging almost a goal per game and has scored more than half of Liverpool's Premier League goals this season.Like last weekend at Brentford, Isak didn't necessarily set the game alight, but again it was another crucial goal from the Swede. His strike gave Liverpool breathing space against a Brighton team that had 64% possession and actually ended the game with a higher xG than Andoni Iraola's side.In the end, Liverpool saw the game out and this was arguably their finest display in the league under Iraola, who secured his first league win at Anfield at the fourth time of asking.Only Erling Haaland (nine) has scored more Premier League goals this season than  Isak and when Liverpool signed him from Newcastle these were the numbers they expected.During Isak's struggles in an injury-plagued campaign in 2025-26, the belief inside the club was that this was a long-term signing and any judgement would be reserved for when he was fully fit. Judging by recent performances, that patience is proving to be warranted."Today, the performance was really good against a really good team," Isak said."The first half is really what we want to be about - winning balls and the intensity."The exciting thing for Iraola and Liverpool is that Isak is nowhere near his best yet, and that should be a cause of worry for the rest of the top flight. It is Arsenal next up in the league."Alex [Isak] is threatening, especially if we can get him in those positions and we can provide him good crosses. In this case, it's a matter of Bradley [Barcola] winning the duel and being faster than the opposition to get us in that position," said Iraola.For Iraola, this was a fourth win in a row since the loss to Manchester City at Anfield a fortnight ago.The fans who braved the conditions after Storm Boelo were treated to a display where Liverpool were aggressive from the outset and defended really well to keep a Brighton side that scored 15 league goals in their previous four games at bay.Bar an early chance for Yasin Ayari, which the Swede blazed over, Fabian Hurzeler's side didn't have any major chances of note.Ronald Araujo was again immense and the Liverpool backline kept their fourth clean sheet in eight league games this season.Interestingly, Liverpool's possession of 35.6% was their second lowest on record (since 2003-04) in a Premier League home win. Iraola's Bournemouth side certainly preferred to have less of the ball and this was a reminder that, with the quality at his disposal going forward, Liverpool are perhaps fine with teams coming to Anfield and having more of the ball, especially if it means the opposition aren't set up in a low block.Both Florian Wirtz and Barcola were excellent and Cody Gakpo threatened all afternoon too, with Wirtz unlucky not to be credited for the goal when his strike took a deflection off Pascal Gross and gave Liverpool the lead. Slowly but surely, his confidence is increasing in a Liverpool shirt and it is clear to see the impact he has on a game. The German just needs the numbers to improve on his end and Liverpool will hope that he isn’t set for a spell on the sidelines after he was substituted in the second half."Unfortunately, he had to leave the pitch with a small twist of the ankle," said Iraola."It doesn't look very big but we are playing every three days so we need to see where he is."As for Barcola, there is a style to his play that can energise a crowd and the way he won possession for Isak's goal felt like it ticked off exactly what Iraola wanted with the high press and sheer desire to win the ball back.That left Isak to finish instinctively and Barcola imitated Isak's celebration, just like they did last weekend in west London, as Liverpool moved up to fourth.Theirs is a combination that cost the Reds a total of £248m but if they can keep on combining and winning games, that will do just fine for Iraola and Liverpool.

schema.headline: Liverpool beat Brighton: Alexander Isak living up to price tag as Liverpool's winning run continues

title: Girl, four, dies after fall from tower block in Barking
description: A four-year-old girl has died after falling from a tower block in east London.The Metropolitan Police said officers were called to the scene at an add
body: A four-year-old girl has died after falling from a tower block in east London.The Metropolitan Police said officers were called to the scene at an address in St Paul's Road, Barking, at about 11:00 BST on Saturday morning, following reports that a child had fallen from height. Paramedics from the London Ambulance Service gave first aid and the child was taken to hospital, but later died from her injuries.A Met spokesperson said the incident was not believed to be suspicious."Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with the child's family and loved ones at this incredibly difficult time," they said."An investigation into the circumstances surrounding this tragic incident is ongoing. However, at this time, the incident is not believed to be suspicious."We urge anyone with information about the incident to contact police on 101, quoting CAD 2424/24OCT."Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook,, external X,, external and Instagram., external Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
